leadTime.label: lead time
leadTime.explanation: {zone} was flagged at {flagged}, using only the hotspots seen up to then. In the recorded satellite data the first hotspot within {radius} km of it came at {reached}.
leadTime.range: {exact} at 3 km, between 5 and 8 hours at 2 to 5 km: one satellite pixel decides the arrival, and the model was tuned on this fire. Hence a round figure.
leadTime.definition: Lead time is the time between the first forecast that put {zone} in the fire's predicted path, using only satellite hotspots observed up to that moment, and the first satellite hotspot within {radius} km of its outline. It is computed from satellite data only and says nothing about when the authorities warned anyone.

landing.title: HackFire: evacuation calls ahead of a wildfire

hero.title: Call every resident in a wildfire's path and know who needs help
hero.lead: HackFire predicts where a wildfire is heading, phones the residents in its path with a way out that avoids the fire, and shows the emergency coordinator who is leaving, who did not answer and who needs rescue.
hero.event: Built at HackBarna 2026 for the Norrsken and Deepfire AI for Wildfire challenge, track 4: values at risk.
hero.shot: The HackFire dashboard on a phone during the replay: satellite hotspots, the predicted spread, residents pinned by triage state and a count for each state.
hero.caption: The coordinator's dashboard replaying 23 July 2026, with sample residents.

leadTime.start: {zone} flagged in the fire's predicted path
leadTime.body: With only the satellite hotspots seen up to {flagged} on 23 July 2026, HackFire put {zone} in the fire's predicted path. The first hotspot within {radius} km of the estate came at {reached}.
leadTime.caveat: Computed from satellite data only. It says nothing about when anyone was warned.
leadTime.title: About {hours} hours of lead time
leadTime.range: Between {min} and {max} hours depending on the distance used ({near}–{far} km)
leadTime.window: First hotspot within {far} km at {early}, within {near} km at {late}
leadTime.why: A single satellite pixel of medium confidence decides the minute the fire counts as arrived, and the prediction's constants were tuned on this same fire. It has not yet been tested on another one.

problem.title: The fire we replay
problem.body: On 23 July 2026 the Burgohondo wildfire in Ávila ran 3 km in 40 minutes and reached the La Atalaya housing estate in El Tiemblo. Between 1,200 and 1,300 people were evacuated from it and 5 homes were destroyed.
problem.gap: Public alerts are one-way. ES-Alert sends one message to a whole area and cannot hear back: the coordinator does not know who has left, who never got the message and who cannot move.

how.title: How it works
how.lead: The afternoon of 23 July 2026, in a short loop. Choose a step to go to that moment.
how.fireTitle: The fire and where it is heading
how.fireBody: Satellite hotspots from Deepfire, fresh in yellow and older in red, and a predicted spread from the speed and heading of the front.
how.zonesBody: The prediction is crossed with towns, housing estates, care homes and schools from OpenStreetMap. Each place gets a time to impact.
how.callTitle: A call to every resident at risk
how.callBody: The voice agent gives each resident a way out that avoids the fire and asks whether they can leave on their own.
how.triageBody: Each answer becomes a state on the map. Evacuees get a route to a safe point; each rescue goes to the fire crew with the way to the door.
how.honest: Illustrative animation: real satellite hotspots from 23 July; example residents and call.
how.map: Animated map of the fire of 23 July 2026 near El Tiemblo, Ávila.
how.call: Example call to a resident of La Atalaya
how.waiting: The calls start once a zone is in the predicted path.
how.agentLine: I'm calling from the emergency coordination about the fire. You need to leave now for San Martín de Valdeiglesias.
how.agentAsk: Can you leave on your own?

outcomes.title: Every call ends in one of three states
outcomes.evacuating: Leaving on their own, with a route to a safe point that avoids the fire.
outcomes.no_answer: Nobody picked up. The agent calls again, and the coordinator knows where to send a patrol.
outcomes.needs_rescue: Cannot leave alone. Ranked by time to impact and sent to the fire crew with the route to the door.
outcomes.lead: Calls start from the prediction, hours ahead, while the cell towers still work.

stack.title: What it is built on
stack.deepfireBody: Satellite hotspots for the replay, and the fires burning right now for live mode.
stack.spreadBody: A cone from the front's velocity, estimated from the last three hours of hotspots, using only what had been observed at each moment.
stack.routingBody: Routes by car and on foot that avoid the predicted fire. The fire crew's route avoids only what has already burned.
stack.voiceBody: Two voice agents, both thinking with NVIDIA Nemotron Super 3: one talks to residents, the other answers the coordinator.
stack.placesBody: Towns, housing estates, care homes, schools, health centres and roads in the fire's path.

note.title: A note on the real fire
note.body: The demo replays a real event from July 2026 in which people lost their homes. Our one headline figure, lead time, is computed from satellite data only: the gap between the moment the system flags a zone as at risk and the moment hotspots reach it. We make no claim about what the emergency services did or when.

truth.title: What is real and what is not
truth.real: The fire: Deepfire's satellite hotspots of 23 July 2026, and in live mode the fires burning now in Spain with Deepfire's ELMFIRE spread simulations. The places and roads, from OpenStreetMap. The routes, from openrouteservice. The voice agents, which are real AI agents on SLNG.
truth.fiction: The residents and their homes, what they answer, the calls in the replay, the evacuations and the crew alerts. Nobody near the real fire was called. Real people, real registries and official evacuation plans would come with the emergency services.
